headline: Coons carries Sussex as Delaware moves 12 points toward Democrats
dek: Chris Coons won a fourth Senate term by 27 points. All three of Delaware's counties moved toward Democrats by similar amounts, and Republican Sussex County voted for him for the first time.
summary: Coons won by 27.1 points, a 12.4-point move from 2024, and Sussex County flipped from Trump to the Democrat.

paras.text: Chris Coons won a fourth term in the U.S. Senate on Tuesday. It was the first time since 2010 that Delaware Democrats had won all three of the state's counties in his race. With 99 percent of the expected vote counted, the Democrat led Republican Mike Katz 240,347 to 137,764, a margin of 27.1 points. Kamala Harris carried Delaware by 14.7 points in 2024, so the state moved 12.4 points toward the Democrats.

The three counties moved by nearly the same amount: Sussex by 14 points, Kent by 13 and New Castle by 12. That is a little less than the typical county across the country this year, which moved 14 points toward Democrats. But in a state with only three counties, a uniform move was enough to flip one of them.
Sussex breaks a long Republican streak

Donald Trump carried Sussex County, the state's southern and coastal county, by 11.0 points in 2024. Coons won it by 2.9. WHYY reported that the last time Sussex County voted in favor of any Democrat for a statewide or federal position was in 2012. WHYY's Return Day coverage noted that it was the first time U.S. Sen. Chris Coons won in the county since he was elected in 2010.

The shift showed up further down the ballot too. Spotlight Delaware reported that Democrats flipped three seats in Camden, Long Neck and Middletown. In Sussex, the winner was Gregg Lindner, who campaigned on issues that have become common refrains among many Sussex County residents — lacking infrastructure, healthcare access and environmental concerns. WHYY reported that voters in District 5 flipped a seat, electing Democrat Jill Hicks to the Sussex County Council. Not every contest was competitive: several Republicans in Sussex County also ran without a challenger.

The county's voter rolls have changed too. According to WHYY, about 40% of Sussex County voters were registered as Republicans in 2020, and that percentage dropped to about 35% this year. The Democratic share fell as well, from 36% to 31%. Evelyn Brady, the state Democratic chair, told WHYY that Sussex County was part of a larger national "blue wave."
A one-sided race in a wave year

Katz, a physician, served in the state Senate as a Democrat for one term from 2009 to 2013. He ran for U.S. Senate in 2024 as the Independent Party candidate, finishing third, then won this year's Republican primary as the Delaware Republican Party's endorsed candidate.

The candidates shared a stage once, at a Rotary Club of Wilmington forum on Oct. 22, the first day of early voting. Spotlight Delaware reported that Coons called the race a "job interview" and urged voters not to "take a risk on an untested candidate." Katz argued that 16 years of Coons in office had left Delaware "unaffordable" and "dying." Delaware Public Media reported that Katz also pushed for a formal debate between himself and Coons, repeatedly. NBC10 reported that Coons has criticized President Donald Trump's tariffs and described the war with Iran as illegal, and that he campaigned on fighting Medicaid cuts.

The Senate race was part of a broader Democratic night. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that Democrats swept every statewide race in the First State on election night, flipped Republican seats in the statehouse in all three counties, and gained supermajorities in both the state Senate and House of Representatives for the first time since 1992. WHYY said legislative Democrats won running on quality-of-life issues. The Inquirer also reported that more Delawareans voted in this election cycle than in any midterm since 2018.
Who moved, and why the count can't fully say

Counties are not voters, and with only three of them the charts beside this section are thin. Each county falls in its own 2024 band, though, and the pattern is clear. Sussex, the one county Trump won by 10 to 30 points, cast 30 percent of the vote and moved 13.9 points. Kent, which Harris won by under 10, cast 17 percent and moved 12.8. New Castle, home to Wilmington and the one county Harris won by 30 or more, cast 53 percent and moved 12.4. The reddest county moved most and the bluest least, but only 1.5 points separate them. That is close to an even swing across the state. All three counties fall in the same size band (50,000 to 250,000 votes) and the same turnout band, so those charts show a single bar each. The page has no Census breakdown for Delaware.

Turnout fell, as it usually does in a midterm. The three counties cast 378,111 votes, 74 percent of the 511,697 cast in 2024. Sussex held up best, at 78 percent of its 2024 total. New Castle came in at 72 percent and Kent at 72 percent.

County totals cannot separate voters who changed their minds from voters who stayed home or newly showed up. Two clues point in different directions. If the swing came only from Republicans skipping the election, the biggest moves would more likely be where turnout fell most. Instead, Sussex, where turnout fell least, moved most. That cuts against a pure turnout explanation. On the other hand, Delaware LIVE, working from the state's list of who had voted, reported that Democrats make up roughly 41% of Delaware's registered voters but accounted for slightly more than half of ballots cast through mid-afternoon. That suggests a turnout gap played a part. Sussex's changing population adds a third possibility: some of its 2026 voters were not on the rolls in 2024. The county numbers are consistent with all three explanations and cannot say how much each contributed.
